statement: URL discovery is a continuous, unbounded process, not a one-time registration: Google finds URLs via internal/external links, submitted XML sitemaps, manual URL Inspection ("Request Indexing") submissions, IndexNow pings, redirects, and referrals from other Google properties, and states the vast majority of indexed pages are found and added automatically rather than manually submitted.

Industry consensus (T3): orphan pages (no internal/external inbound links, absent from any sitemap) are the single most common reason a legitimate page is never discovered; crawl-budget-constrained large sites (>1M URLs) disproportionately suffer discovery failures in deep site sections. A frequently-misunderstood distinction: a robots.txt Disallow rule blocks crawling of a directory, not necessarily indexing — a disallowed URL can still be indexed with no snippet if linked from elsewhere [T1]. statement: Google operates a two-wave (queued) crawl/render model — it first crawls raw HTML and extracts links/metadata without executing JavaScript, then separately queues the page for rendering (which can happen seconds to weeks later) via the Web Rendering Service, an evergreen continuously-updated Chromium. Non-search AI crawlers (GPTBot, OAI-SearchBot, ClaudeBot, Claude-SearchBot, PerplexityBot) are documented as HTTP-fetch-based only, and independent server-log analyses consistently show them requesting only the initial HTML document with no corresponding requests for bundled JS assets.
context: Google Search Central's "Understand the JavaScript SEO basics" documentation describes this crawl → render → index pipeline and states rendering is deferred and queued separately [T1]. Bing documents a similar rendering pipeline with less public detail on wave timing [T1]. The AI-crawler non-rendering finding is T3/T4: reproducible via log analysis and consistent across independent audits, but not officially confirmed as a permanent architectural guarantee by OpenAI, Anthropic, or Perplexity — it could change without notice. Industry consensus: the rendering queue historically introduced indexing delay for JS-dependent content; Google has narrowed this gap over time but measurable lag is still found in large-scale crawl studies. Common failure modes: content only appearing after client-side JS execution being invisible to non-rendering crawlers; render-blocking resources blocked via robots.txt preventing WRS from seeing a complete page (which Google explicitly warns against); timeouts on JS-heavy single-page apps; content requiring user interaction to appear, which no crawler (including Googlebot's WRS) simulates.
uncertainty: T1 for Google's documented crawl/render separation and evergreen Chromium; T3/T4 for the claim that AI crawlers never execute JavaScript at all — this is a consistently observed pattern (log analysis, >=2 independent corroborations) but not a vendor-confirmed permanent guarantee, so it is held at medium rather than high confidence and could need revision if a vendor changes behavior.

Common failure modes: infinite loading spinners with no server-renderable fallback; JS errors halting execution before primary content mounts; IntersectionObserver-based reveal that never fires without real scroll events; content gated behind service-worker registration, which crawlers do not persist across visits the way a returning human browser would.
uncertainty: T1 for Google's documented execution constraints (no interaction simulation, existence of a timeout, the named soft-404/error failure modes); T3/T4 for the exact timeout threshold (never disclosed) and for the claim that AI crawlers skip this stage entirely, which is inferred from consistent absence of asset requests in server logs rather than a vendor statement.

statement: Google selects one canonical URL from a cluster of perceived duplicate/near-duplicate URLs using multiple weighted signals (rel="canonical" hints, redirects, internal linking patterns, sitemap inclusion, HTTPS preference, shorter/simpler URL structure) and explicitly states no single signal is decisive; rel="canonical" is a hint, not a directive, and Google can override an author-declared canonical when other signals strongly disagree.
context: developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/canonicalization and .../consolidate-duplicate-urls explicitly enumerate the signal list and the "hint not directive" framing [T1]. Search Console reports a distinct "Google chose different canonical than user" status, confirming this override happens in practice at scale [T1]. Cross-domain canonicalization (pointing a canonical tag to a different domain, e.g. for syndication) is supported and documented [T1]. Industry consensus (T3): conflicting canonicalization signals (a self-referencing canonical contradicted by a sitemap or by internal links pointing elsewhere) are among the most frequently cited causes of "Duplicate, Google chose different canonical than user" in large-site audits. Common failure modes: parameter-based URL variants (tracking params, session IDs, sort/filter facets) without consistent canonical tags; paginated series all self-canonicalizing to page 1 (Google deprecated formal rel=prev/next support in 2019 but paginated series still need sound internal signals) [T1/T2]; HTTP/HTTPS or www/non-www variants both crawlable and inconsistently internally linked; canonical tags pointing to a non-indexable (noindexed, blocked, or redirecting) target, which Google effectively treats as a broken hint.

statement: Content extraction is the step where a search or AI system separates "main content" from templated boilerplate (navigation, footers, ads, related-content widgets) within the rendered DOM; Google has never published its exact algorithm, but data-nosnippet and nosnippet directives confirm a main-content/boilerplate distinction exists at the element level, and RAG-based AI-answer engines (ChatGPT Search, Perplexity, Claude web search) must perform an equivalent extraction step before passing fetched content to their generating model.
context: Semantic HTML5 elements (<main>, <article>, <nav>, <aside>, <header>, <footer>) are part of the W3C/WHATWG HTML Living Standard and provide machine-parseable structural hints, though Google has not confirmed these tags are a primary extraction signal versus one of several heuristics (text density, DOM position, boilerplate-pattern matching common in open-source extraction libraries like Mozilla's Readability or the academic "boilerpipe" algorithm) [T4 — plausible inference from web-standards design intent, not a Google-confirmed extraction mechanism]. None of the RAG-based AI vendors publish their extraction algorithm, but all describe "well-structured," "informative" content as preferred inputs in public guidance [T2 — vendor statements, not algorithmic disclosure]. Industry consensus (T3): content interleaved with ads/widgets/navigation, or requiring interaction to reveal (accordions/tabs not present in initial DOM), is more prone to extraction failure or truncation than clearly demarcated main-content blocks. Common failure modes: primary content interleaved character-by-character with navigation/sidebar markup in DOM order (even if visually separated by CSS); critical information inside accordion/tab components collapsed by default and only rendered on click (invisible to non-interactive crawlers); content split across multiple paginated "page views" of one logical article with no "view all" alternative.
